newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Balladur urges EU pact on growth.
newsitem.headline: France's Balladur urges EU pact on growth.

text.p: Ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur offered his services on Sunday to the beleagured government of President Jacques Chirac and urged the European Union to agree to pro-growth policies once a single currency is in place.

"I'm thinking of myself," the Gaullist deputy replied when asked in a broadcast interview what he meant when he said individuals must be prepared to assume responsibility if they wished to take part in important decisions for France's future.

Balladur, who was succeeded as prime minister by Alain Juppe last year following his unsuccessful bid for the French presidency against fellow Gaullist Chirac, has become a vocal critic of the Juppe government from the sidelines.

With Juppe's approval rating at record lows, Balladur has made no secret of his eagerness to return to the spotlight, but Sunday's statement was the most vivid indication so far of his interest in returning to government.

In an interview on Europe 1 radio, Balladur said he favoured the centre-right government's policies in general but wanted to "go farther in some areas" to stimulate growth, company activity and consumer confidence.
He said the EU needed to take two steps to flourish after the launch of the single currency -- the Euro -- set for 1999.
"The European member states must sign a contract for European growth which would stress two themes -- the currency -- the Euro -- and taxes and payroll deductions," he said.

He said such a contract should make clear what model the states wanted for the EU central bank and should also promote coordinated cuts in taxes and payroll deductions to encourage growth across the bloc.
"I do not want all of the European states to be rigorously alike but If we want Europe to be a region of prosperity, which it is not at the moment, we must take care of these two problems," he said.
Concerning taxes, he said the EU contract should enable member states to "lower their taxes together".

Concerning a central bank, he said he preferred a model based on the American Federal Reserve which focuses on jobs and growth over that of the German Bundesbank "which is obsessed with inflation in a world where there is no inflation".

"I am a very strong supporter of the Franco-German partnership which is the motor of Europe, but Germany must admit that growth is insufficient," he said. Interest and tax rates were too high and regulation too complex, he said.

Balladur said he also favoured cutting red tape in France's byzantine labour code. "We should put some order and clarity into a legislative and bureaucratic apparatus which is often incomprehensible," he said.
But with unemployment at a record 12.6 percent, he said he did not want to take away job protection measures.
